ostentatious

ah-sten-TAY-shus · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Ostentatious is designed to impress others through a showy display of wealth or importance.

The senator's critics accused him of an ostentatious use of taxpayer funds after photos surfaced of his gold-plated office chair.

Example

The wedding's ostentatious centerpiece -- a six-foot ice sculpture of the couple's initials -- cost more than most guests' monthly rent.

The ice sculpture wasn't a modest decoration -- it was an extravagant display clearly meant to impress every guest, exactly what ostentatious describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

showy: Showy means designed to catch the eye and pull attention to itself — bold feathers, a big gesture, a splashy cover. Ostentatious narrows the motive: it is a showy display of wealth or importance staged so that others will be impressed. Showy is about attention; ostentatious is about status.

conspicuous: Conspicuous just means easy to notice — a conspicuous empty seat, a conspicuous stain on a white shirt. It says nothing about intent. Ostentatious is deliberately conspicuous: a display of wealth or importance arranged to impress. Things become conspicuous by accident; nothing is ostentatious by accident.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

understated: subtle and not obviously showy

modest: not showy or elaborate; simple

Where it sits · how excessive the display is — fancy → ostentatious → extravagant

fancy vs. ostentatious: Something fancy is simply elaborate or nice, without the deliberate showing-off implied by ostentatious.

extravagant vs. ostentatious: Something extravagant goes beyond mere showiness into wastefully excessive spending, a step further than ostentatious.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — os-

Prefix — os-: toward, in front of (Latin ob-, which becomes os- before t)

Root — tentat

Root — tentat: to stretch out, to display again and again (from Latin ostentare, 'to display,' a repeated-action form of tendere, 'to stretch')

Suffix — -ious

Suffix — -ious: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Ostentatious comes from os- ('toward,' the form Latin ob- takes before t) + tentat ('to stretch out, to display,' from Latin ostentare, a repeated-action form of tendere, 'to stretch') + -ious -- as if stretching something out in front of an audience, again and again. The same root tendere gives us the everyday word pretend, literally 'to stretch forth' a false claim.

Use the root in a new word: pretend

Use the root in a new word: pretend: The children loved to pretend the backyard was a pirate ship sailing rough seas.

Root Check

Word Choice

Ostentatious specifically points to a display of wealth or status meant to impress -- unlike gaudy, which criticizes something's tacky appearance regardless of cost, or bravado, which describes a person's showy confidence rather than their possessions.
